workings: Given \(3\sin P + 4\cos Q = 6\) and \(4\sin Q + 3\cos P = 1\), with \(P + Q + R = \pi\).
Square the first: \(9\sin^2 P + 24\sin P\cos Q + 16\cos^2 Q = 36\)
Square the second: \(16\sin^2 Q + 24\sin Q\cos P + 9\cos^2 P = 1\)
Add them: \(9(\sin^2 P + \cos^2 P) + 16(\sin^2 Q + \cos^2 Q) + 24(\sin P\cos Q + \cos P\sin Q) = 37\)
Using \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\) and \(\sin(P+Q) = \sin P\cos Q + \cos P\sin Q\): \(9 + 16 + 24\sin(P+Q) = 37\)
Reject \(P+Q = \frac{\pi}{6}\): then \(P < \frac{\pi}{6}\), so \(3\sin P < \frac{3}{2}\), while \(4\cos Q \le 4\), giving \(3\sin P + 4\cos Q < \frac{11}{2} < 6\), contradicting the first equation.
note: Solving the original two-equation system numerically gives \(P = 2.0115387682\), \(Q = 0.6064551098\), \(R = 0.5235987756 = \frac{\pi}{6}\), satisfying both equations exactly. A numerical scan confirms the rejected branch caps at \(5.5 < 6\).

workings: \(E = \tan A + \cot A + 1 = \frac{\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A}{\sin A\cos A} + 1\)
note: Note \(\tan A + \cot A\) alone is short by exactly \(1\); the printed value \(\tan A + \cot A\) is the trap for anyone who drops the \(+1\).

workings: \(\sin^4 x + \cos^4 x = (\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x)^2 - 2\sin^2 x\cos^2 x = 1 - 2\sin^2 x\cos^2 x\)
\(\sin^6 x + \cos^6 x = (\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x)^3 - 3\sin^2 x\cos^2 x(\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x) = 1 - 3\sin^2 x\cos^2 x\)
The coefficient of \(\sin^2 x\cos^2 x\) is \(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} = 0\), so the difference is a constant, independent of \(x\).
Let \(c = \cos 2x\). Then \(\cos^2 x = \frac{1+c}{2}\), \(\sin^2 x = \frac{1-c}{2}\), so \(\tan^2 x = \frac{1-c}{1+c}\).
note: A numerical root scan over \(\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) finds exactly one solution, \(x = 0.955316618\), at which \(\cos 2x = -\frac{1}{3}\) and \(\cos 4x = -0.7777777778\).

workings: \(E = 13 - 4\cos^6\theta\), valid for every \(\theta\) (the restriction to \(\left(\frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) is not needed).
note: Two of the printed alternatives, \(13 - 4\cos^4\theta + 2\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta\) and \(13 - 4\cos^2\theta + 6\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta\), are algebraically IDENTICAL to each other: their difference is \(4\cos^2\theta\left(1 - \sin^2\theta - \cos^2\theta\right) = 0\). They agree to 15 decimal places at all six test angles. Neither equals the expression, so the answer is still unambiguous, but the option set contains a printed twin.

workings: \(P = \cos\frac{\pi}{2^2}\cos\frac{\pi}{2^3}\cdots\cos\frac{\pi}{2^{10}}\cdot\sin\frac{\pi}{2^{10}}\), which has nine cosine factors (\(k = 2\) to \(k = 10\)).
Use \(2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha = \sin 2\alpha\), starting at the right-hand end.
Each cosine is absorbed the same way: the coefficient halves and the angle doubles.
note: Direct evaluation gives \(0.001953125 = \frac{1}{512}\) to 40 decimal places. Counting the cosine factors is the whole question: \(k = 2,3,\ldots,10\) is nine factors, not ten, so the power is \(2^{9}\).

workings: For \(a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta\) the maximum over real \(\theta\) is \(\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\).
note: A fine scan over \([0, 2\pi]\) plus a refined stationary point gives \(4.3588989435406740 = \sqrt{19}\). The value \(\sqrt{34}\) is what a careless \(\sqrt{3^2 + 5^2}\) gives, ignoring the phase shift.

workings: Write the equation as \((k+1)\tan^2 x - \sqrt{2}\lambda\tan x - (1-k) = 0\), a quadratic in \(\tan x\) whose roots are \(\tan\alpha\) and \(\tan\beta\).
note: Checked numerically across several values of \(k\): \(\lambda = 10\) gives \(\tan^2(\alpha+\beta) = 50\) for every admissible \(k\), while \(5\) gives \(12.5\), \(5\sqrt{2}\) gives \(25\) and \(10\sqrt{2}\) gives \(100\). The \(k\)-independence is what makes the question well posed.
Direct evaluation gives \(0.3535533906 = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\) to 40 decimal places.
